finding: When the owner judged each method's top 100 unjudged pictures, the classifier trained on 100 verdicts was clearly ahead of the shipped near-neighbour vote on neither tag tested: on hand it was clearly behind (83 of 100 confirmed against 94 of 98, p = 0.005), and on jewelry it was ahead but not clearly (39 of 74 against 28 of 76, p = 0.07), reversing on hand the 26-point lead idea 4 measured on already-judged pictures.

followUps.title: Short judging games of about 110 pictures on two or three clear-cut, less common tags
followUps.body: This round asked the owner to judge about 290 pictures per tag, and they stopped after one and a half tags, so only two tags were measured, one going each way. A shorter game keeps each method's 30 best pictures, drops pictures that look almost the same as one already kept, and adds 30 pictures chosen at random so the result can be compared with plain chance. That makes about 110 pictures a tag. The prototype for this already exists in this round (short_list.py). Pick tags that are easy to say yes or no to, and that the automatic tagger puts on well under half the library, unlike hand at 72%. A classifier that is clearly ahead on two or more of them would reopen the question; one that is not would settle it.

followUps.title: Check how consistently a person judges a tag before teaching it from their answers
followUps.body: Pictures with a known earlier answer were mixed into each judging game. On jewelry, the owner gave the same yes again on only 6 of 11 pictures they had said yes to before, against 14 of 16 on hand. Any method taught from 100 answers inherits that noise. Before teaching a tag, a short game of only already-answered pictures would show how repeatable the tag is. Tags below some agreement level could then be skipped, or have their meaning written down first. This would show whether the classifier's weak showing comes from the method or from the answers it was trained on.

plain.idea: Teach the library a new label from 100 of a person's yes/no answers, then let the person judge, without knowing which method picked them, the 100 new pictures each method thinks most likely carry the label.
settles: Each method picks its 100 best guesses among pictures nobody has answered for that label.
All picks are shuffled together and the person says yes or no to each, not knowing which method picked it.
The idea passes if the new method's picks get clearly more yeses on at least a few labels.
plain.showed: On hands, the existing method's picks were confirmed more often than the new method's. On jewelry the new method did a little better, but not by enough to rule out chance. So the new method was clearly better on neither label, even though an earlier test on already-answered pictures had it well ahead on both.
